mcq.prompt: `void inspect_value(Snapshot s)` and `void inspect_reference(const Snapshot& s)` are each called once with the same named local. How many Snapshot objects are constructed?
choices: One by inspect_value, none by inspect_reference
One by each
None by either — the compiler elides both
One by inspect_reference, none by inspect_value
mcq.explain: A by-value parameter needs its own object, so passing an lvalue copy-constructs one. A const reference aliases the caller's object and constructs nothing. Elision cannot help the by-value case here: there is a named source object that must survive the call, so there is a genuine copy to make.

mcq.prompt: Given `std::vector<double> prices;`, which of `auto copied = prices;`, `auto& aliased = prices;`, `const auto& read_only = prices;` allocates?
choices: All three
Only `auto& aliased`
Only `auto copied`
None — auto never copies a container
mcq.explain: Plain auto deduces std::vector<double>, so `copied` is an independent vector: a new allocation plus an element-by-element copy. Both reference forms bind to the existing object and allocate nothing. The hazard is that all three lines look equally cheap — the deduction, not the syntax, decides whether a copy happens.

mcq.prompt: What does move-assignment have to do that move-construction does not?
choices: Copy the source's elements before taking ownership
Dispose of the destination's existing resource first
Leave the source unchanged
Allocate storage for the destination
mcq.explain: Move construction builds a fresh object, so there is nothing to release. Move assignment targets an object that already exists and may already own a resource, which must be disposed of before taking the source's — otherwise it leaks. Neither operation allocates or copies elements, and both leave the source in a valid but unspecified state, so it is emphatically not unchanged.

mcq.prompt: A hand-written move constructor copies the source's pointer member but does not null it. What is the consequence?
choices: The source becomes unusable but is otherwise harmless
The move silently degrades into a copy
Both objects' destructors release the same resource, which is undefined behavior
The destination's destructor is skipped, leaking the resource
mcq.explain: There are now two owners of one allocation, and a moved-from object is not destroyed — its destructor still runs at the end of its lifetime. Both will release the same pointer, which is a double free. `std::exchange(other.data_, nullptr)` returns the old value while installing the null in one step, which is why the idiom reads so cleanly in an initializer list.

mcq.prompt: Why does a move constructor include `if (this != &other)` in its *assignment* form but usually not in its constructor form?
choices: Because a constructor cannot be called on an already-constructed object, so self-move-construction cannot arise
Because assignment is slower and the check pays for itself
Because the constructor's initializer list is exception-safe and the assignment body is not
Because the check is required by the standard for assignment operators
mcq.explain: `buffer = std::move(buffer)` is expressible and would otherwise delete the resource and then try to take it from the object it just emptied. A constructor is initializing a new object, so there is no way for the destination and source to be the same object. The standard requires no such check — it is the type's own way of keeping its invariant under a legal but odd call.

mcq.prompt: Inside `void relay(Order&& order) { sink(order); }` with overloads `sink(const Order&)` and `sink(Order&&)`, which overload is selected?
choices: sink(Order&&), because order's type is Order&&
sink(Order&&), but only at -O2
It is ambiguous
sink(const Order&), because the expression `order` is an lvalue
mcq.explain: A variable expression is an lvalue even when the variable's declared type is an rvalue reference — the name gives repeated access to a particular object, so binding it to a move overload would let one call silently gut it. Writing `sink(std::move(order))` marks the point where relay intentionally passes the value onward. Declared type and value category are different questions.

mcq.prompt: Which value category does `std::move(order)` produce, and what does that mean?
choices: A prvalue — a fresh value with no identity yet
An lvalue — it still names the same object
An xvalue — an expiring value identifying an object whose resources may be reused
It has no value category; std::move is a compiler intrinsic
mcq.explain: An xvalue has identity (it designates a specific object) and is movable (it is treated as expiring), which is exactly the combination a move overload wants. A prvalue is the category of a temporary such as `Order{42}`, which usually initializes its destination directly rather than being moved from. std::move is an ordinary library function template, not an intrinsic.

mcq.prompt: `sink(Order{});` with overloads `sink(const Order&)` and `sink(Order&&)`. Which is selected?
choices: sink(const Order&)
sink(Order&&)
Ambiguous
sink(const Order&), because a temporary is const
mcq.explain: `Order{}` is a prvalue, so the rvalue-reference overload is the better match. Temporaries are not const — that misconception comes from the fact that a const lvalue reference *can* bind to one, which is what made pre-move C++ work at all; it just is not the preferred binding when an rvalue overload exists.

mcq.prompt: What does std::move do at runtime?
choices: Nothing — it is a cast that changes the expression's value category and generates no instructions
Transfers the object's resources to a destination
Marks the object as moved-from so later reads can be diagnosed
Calls the type's move constructor
mcq.explain: std::move is conceptually a static_cast<T&&>: it changes what overload resolution sees and compiles to zero instructions. The actual transfer is done by whichever constructor or assignment operator that resolution then selects. Nothing is marked — Clang-Tidy's bugprone-use-after-move is static analysis, not a runtime flag.

mcq.prompt: `const Order original; auto copy = std::move(original);` for a type with both a copy and a move constructor. What runs?
choices: The move constructor; std::move strips const
The move constructor, with the const object modified through a hidden const_cast
Neither — the initialization is ill-formed
The copy constructor; std::move preserves const, producing const Order&&, which cannot bind to Order&&
mcq.explain: std::move produces a const Order&& here, and the move constructor's Order&& parameter cannot bind to it, so the best viable overload is the copy constructor taking const Order&. The request to move was made and silently refused — the same thing happens for a type with no move operation at all. Do not add const to an object that must transfer ownership.

mcq.prompt: What may you assume about a moved-from standard-library object?
choices: It is empty
It is equal to a default-constructed object of its type
It is destructible and assignable; its value is unspecified
It must not be touched again in any way
mcq.explain: The guarantee is valid-but-unspecified: destroy it, assign it a fresh value, or call an operation with no preconditions such as clear(). Implementations commonly do leave a moved-from std::string empty, which is exactly why relying on it is a portability trap. Nor is the object off-limits — it still has a lifetime and its destructor will still run.

mcq.prompt: Why must a hand-written move operation leave the source in a state that is safe to destroy?
choices: Because the compiler inserts a destructor call immediately after any move
Because a moved-from object is not destroyed by the move; its destructor still runs at the end of its lifetime
Because the standard requires moved-from objects to compare equal to their default state
Because otherwise the destination cannot take ownership
mcq.explain: Moving transfers a resource; it does not end the source's lifetime. The source is still a live object whose destructor runs at its normal time, so if the move left it holding a pointer the destination now owns, that destructor performs a second release. The destructor is not called early, and no equality requirement exists.

mcq.section: Elision: RVO, NRVO, and guaranteed elision
mcq.prompt: `Order make_direct(int id) { return Order{id}; }` where Order has both copy and move constructors deleted. What happens?
choices: It fails to compile: a return requires an accessible copy or move constructor
It compiles at -O2 but not at -O0
It compiles, but a move is still performed and then optimized away
It compiles: returning a prvalue of the function's result type constructs directly in the caller's result object
mcq.explain: Guaranteed copy elision (C++17) is a language rule, not an optimization: no separate temporary Order ever needs to exist, so no copy or move constructor is required or called. -O0 does not restore a move, because there was never one to elide in the pre-C++17 sense — temporary materialization simply supplies an object only where one is needed.

mcq.section: Elision: RVO, NRVO, and guaranteed elision
mcq.prompt: Why is `return std::move(local);` usually a pessimization?
choices: std::move adds a runtime cast instruction on the return path
It makes the returned object const, so a copy is selected instead
It prevents the implicit move that a bare `return local;` would perform
It turns an NRVO candidate into an xvalue, forcing a move where direct construction was possible
mcq.explain: A bare `return local;` lets the compiler construct the local directly in the return destination (NRVO), and if NRVO does not happen the return expression is move-eligible anyway — so you get the move as a fallback for free. Writing std::move gives up the better case to guarantee the worse one. std::move generates no instructions and does not add const.

mcq.section: Elision: RVO, NRVO, and guaranteed elision
mcq.prompt: Which return statement can NOT use NRVO?
choices: return local; where local is a named local of the result type
return parameter; where parameter is a by-value parameter of the result type
return Order{1};
return local; inside a try block
mcq.explain: A by-value parameter lives in storage the caller helped establish, so it cannot be constructed in the return destination; the return is an implicit move instead. `return Order{1};` is not an NRVO case at all — it is guaranteed elision, which is stronger. Returning a subobject such as `local.member` also cannot use NRVO and copies unless you move it explicitly.

mcq.prompt: `struct Widget { Trace trace; ~Widget() { /* ... */ } };` and then `Widget second = std::move(first);`. Which of Trace's operations runs?
choices: Trace's copy constructor
Trace's move constructor
Neither — Widget is not movable, so this is ill-formed
Trace's move constructor, then its destructor
mcq.explain: The user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor, so no Widget(Widget&&) exists. The generated copy constructor is still viable because its const Widget& parameter binds happily to an xvalue — so the code compiles and silently copies. Nothing warns; this is the failure mode the rule of zero exists to prevent.

mcq.prompt: A class holds only members that already manage their own resources. What does the rule of zero say to declare?
choices: All five special members, defaulted, to state the intent
None of the five special members
The destructor, plus defaulted moves
Deleted copies and defaulted moves
mcq.explain: Declaring none of the five keeps copying, moving, destruction and the conditional noexcept specifications generated correctly and automatically, and keeps them correct as members change. Defaulting all five explicitly is the fallback for when a destructor is genuinely required — it works, but it is five more lines to keep in sync. Deleting copies would be wrong for a type whose members are all copyable.

mcq.section: noexcept moves and the copy fallback
mcq.prompt: A vector must reallocate. Its element type has a copy constructor and a move constructor that is not marked noexcept. What does the vector do with the existing elements?
choices: Moves them, and catches any exception to restore the old buffer
Refuses to compile, because reallocation requires a noexcept move
Moves them, since a move is always preferred when one exists
Copies them, so a throw leaves the original range intact
mcq.explain: std::move_if_noexcept yields a const lvalue in this case, which selects the copy constructor — so if an element operation throws, the original range has not been touched and the strong guarantee survives. Moving and then trying to undo is exactly what cannot work: the already-moved-from sources may be unrestorable. When no copy constructor exists, the library moves anyway and the strong guarantee is waived.

mcq.section: noexcept moves and the copy fallback
mcq.prompt: Where does a defaulted move constructor's noexcept specification come from?
choices: It is always noexcept
It is never noexcept unless written explicitly
It is noexcept if and only if every selected base and member move operation is non-throwing
It matches the destructor's specification
mcq.explain: Defaulted moves are conditionally noexcept: they inherit the promise from the operations they call, so a class of std::string and std::vector members gets a noexcept move for free. That is a strong argument for defaulting rather than hand-writing — a hand-written move that forgets noexcept turns every vector reallocation into full element copies, with an allocation and linear data movement each time.

mcq.prompt: A function stores its argument into a member. Comparing a `const T&` parameter that is then copied into storage against a by-value parameter that is then moved into storage, when the caller passes an existing named object:
choices: The by-value version costs one copy plus one move; the const& version costs one copy
Both cost exactly one copy
The by-value version costs one copy; the const& version costs one copy plus one move
The by-value version avoids the copy entirely
mcq.explain: For an lvalue argument the by-value parameter is copy-constructed and then moved into storage — one copy plus one cheap move — while the const& version performs a single copy. The by-value sink wins on the other side of the trade: a caller passing a prvalue constructs the parameter directly, and an xvalue costs one move, where the const& version would still copy. Choose it when callers commonly hand over values they are finished with.

reading.prompt: This archiving pass was written to avoid copying tiles. What does it print?
reading.explain: The loop variable is `const auto&`, so `tile` has type `const Tile&` and `std::move(tile)` yields a `const Tile&&`. That cannot bind to `Tile(Tile&&)`, so overload resolution falls back to `Tile(const Tile&)` — three copies, zero moves. The tempting reading is that the `std::move` is what makes the loop cheap; in fact `std::move` is only a cast, and here the `const` silently refuses the request. Nothing warns, and the fix is to iterate over a non-const `std::vector<Tile>&` (or take the parameter by value) so the reference is not const.

reading.prompt: What does this print? (`chosen` reports which overload ran.)
reading.explain: `track.add(middle_c)` passes an lvalue and picks the `const Note&` overload. The other two calls pass a prvalue and an xvalue, so both pick `add(Note&&)` — and inside that overload the *expression* `note` is an lvalue even though the parameter's declared type is `Note&&`, so the first `chosen(note)` reports `copy` and only `chosen(std::move(note))` reports `move`. The tempting wrong answer is `cref:copy move/move move/move`, from reading the parameter's declared type as its value category. A name gives repeated access to one object; it never binds to a move overload by itself.

reading.section: Elision: RVO, NRVO, and guaranteed elision
reading.prompt: What does this print? The counters are cumulative across both calls.
reading.explain: `return left ? here : there;` is not an id-expression naming one local, so it is neither an NRVO candidate nor implicitly move-eligible: the conditional yields an lvalue and the return object is copy-constructed — one copy, zero moves, on every compiler. `relabel(Node{5})` then constructs its by-value parameter directly from the prvalue argument (no operation at all), and `return node;` must move because a parameter can never use NRVO — one move — while the prvalue result initialises `tagged` by guaranteed elision. The tempting answer is `0/0 0/0 15`, assuming the compiler elides everything; elision is only ever available where the returned expression names the single return candidate.

reading.prompt: `Handle` is a properly written move-only type. What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: Two rules collide. `Job`'s user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor, and `Job`'s implicit copy constructor is defined as deleted because its `Handle` member has a deleted copy constructor. `std::move(first)` therefore finds only a deleted copy constructor and the program is ill-formed. The tempting reading is that a class made of movable members is movable — it is, right up until any of the five special members is declared. Note the failure mode differs from the chapter's `Widget`: there the member was copyable, so the same suppression compiled and silently copied. Restoring `Job(Job&&) noexcept = default;` (or dropping the destructor) fixes it.

reading.prompt: `collapse` folds one undo entry into the one above it. What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: `collapse(only, only)` binds both references to the same object, so `top = std::move(below)` is a self-move-assignment. The operator deletes `chars_`, then takes `other.chars_` — which is the very pointer it just freed — so `text()` hands a dangling pointer to `strlen`. ASan reports a heap-use-after-free. The tempting reading is that the move assignment is fine because it clears the source with `std::exchange`; clearing the source is necessary but it happens *after* the release, and when source and destination are one object the release has already destroyed what is about to be taken. `if (this != &other)` around the body is what makes the operation total.

reading.section: noexcept moves and the copy fallback
reading.prompt: `Block` and `Clip` differ only in one line. What does this print?
reading.explain: `Block`'s user-declared destructor suppresses its implicit move constructor, so the vector has no move to consider at all and relocates its two existing elements with the still-viable copy constructor. `Clip` declares nothing, so it gets an implicit move constructor that is `noexcept` because `Sample`'s is, and `std::move_if_noexcept` yields an xvalue. The tempting reading is that this is the `noexcept` rule from the chapter — but `Block` never wrote a move to forget `noexcept` on; the destructor deleted the possibility of one. Both routes end in the same place, which is why an empty destructor added for logging can quietly turn container growth into full copies.

writing.prompt: Write a `SampleBlock` that owns `float* samples_` and a `std::size_t count_`, and is both copyable and movable. Satisfy this contract: a copy owns independent storage; both move operations are `noexcept` and leave the source with `count() == 0` (a postcondition this class documents, stronger than valid-but-unspecified); move assignment performs no allocation and is correct when the source and destination are the same object; copy assignment is correct under self-assignment and does not leave the object damaged if the allocation throws.
checklist: Copy construction allocates its own array and copies the elements
Copy assignment allocates the replacement before releasing the old buffer, and is safe under self-assignment
Both move operations are declared noexcept and contain no allocation
Move construction and move assignment both set the source's pointer to null and its count to 0
Move assignment releases the destination's existing buffer and guards against self-move-assignment
The destructor uses delete[] and is safe when the pointer is null
writing.notes: The two assignment operators fail in opposite directions if you skip the guard. Copy assignment that deletes first and allocates second corrupts `*this` when the allocation throws; move assignment that deletes first frees the buffer it is about to take when `block = std::move(block)` is written. The `count() == 0` postcondition is a choice, not a requirement — the library only promises destructible and assignable — but once documented it must actually hold on both move paths, which is exactly what `std::exchange` gives you in one expression. And the `noexcept` is load-bearing: without it a `std::vector<SampleBlock>` would copy every element on every reallocation, since a copy constructor is available here.

writing.prompt: Given the move-only `Reservation` below, add a `Task` holding a `Reservation`, a `std::string`, and a `std::vector<int>`. `Task` must be movable and must not be copyable — and you must achieve both **without writing any special member, not even `= delete`**. Then add a `Schedule` whose `enqueue` takes ownership of a `Task` at a cost of one move. Finally, write an `AuditedTask` variant that genuinely needs a destructor and explain in a comment what that costs and how you pay it back.
checklist: Task declares none of the five special members
A comment explains that Task's copy operations are implicitly defined as deleted because Reservation's are deleted, so move-only is inherited rather than declared
Schedule::enqueue takes its Task by value and moves it into storage
The call site passes std::move(task), and a comment notes that passing it by copy would not compile
AuditedTask declares a destructor and restores the move operations with `noexcept = default`
A comment states that the destructor would otherwise suppress the implicit moves, leaving a type that is neither copyable nor movable
writing.notes: The point of forbidding `= delete` is that move-only is a property a class inherits from its members, not something it announces. Once ownership lives in a suitable member type the enclosing class has nothing left to say, and the rule of zero keeps the conditional `noexcept` specifications correct as the members change. `AuditedTask` shows the price: one declared destructor and the implicit moves are gone, and because the copies were already deleted there is no silent fallback to copying — the type simply stops being usable in a container. That is a better failure than the chapter's `Widget`, which had a copyable member and so compiled and copied instead.

writing.section: Elision: RVO, NRVO, and guaranteed elision
writing.prompt: Write a `Timing` type with all four copy and move operations `= delete`, and then five functions that return a value: one that returns it unconditionally, one that returns one of two results chosen by a branch, and three returning a `std::string` — from a named local, from a by-value parameter, and from a member of a local. Every `Timing` function must compile despite the deleted operations. Comment each return with what actually happens and whether it is guaranteed or optional.
checklist: Timing deletes both copy operations and both move operations, and both Timing-returning functions still compile
A comment identifies prvalue returns as guaranteed elision and a language rule, not an -O level
The branching function returns a prvalue from each branch rather than choosing between two named locals, with a comment on why a conditional over two locals would need a copy
The named-local return is bare, with a comment that NRVO is optional and implicit move is the fallback
The by-value parameter return is identified as an implicit move that cannot use NRVO
The member return uses std::move, with a comment that a subobject was never an elision candidate
writing.notes: The deleted operations turn the exercise into a compile-time proof: if any of the `Timing` returns needed a copy or a move, the file would not build. That is why `measure_branch` has to be written with a `return` in each branch — `return quick ? fast : slow;` over two named locals is an lvalue conditional, which requires a copy constructor and would be rejected outright here (and would silently copy for an ordinary type). The `std::string` functions show the whole spectrum in the other direction: remove `std::move` from the local return, keep it on the subobject return, and leave the parameter return alone because it is already a move.

writing.section: noexcept moves and the copy fallback
writing.prompt: A `std::vector<PacketLog>` copies every existing element each time it outgrows its capacity, even though `PacketLog` holds only types that move cheaply. Diagnose it in a comment, then produce two versions that relocate by moving: one that keeps the destructor, and one that does not need it. Prove the difference with a member that counts copy and move constructions, using `reserve` so the demonstration makes no assumption about the growth factor.
checklist: A comment states that the user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor, leaving the viable copy constructor
The fixed version keeps the destructor and declares all five special members, with the moves written `noexcept = default`
A comment explains that a defaulted move's noexcept is inherited from its members, so `noexcept = default` is checked by the compiler rather than asserted
A second version declares none of the five
The demonstration reserves n, inserts n+1 elements, and reports counts rather than relying on any growth factor
A comment names std::move_if_noexcept as what chooses between the xvalue and the const lvalue
writing.notes: Two different mistakes produce the same symptom, and it is worth being able to tell them apart. A hand-written move that forgets `noexcept` makes `std::move_if_noexcept` hand back a `const` lvalue, so the copy constructor wins; a user-declared destructor removes the move constructor entirely, so there is nothing for `move_if_noexcept` to prefer. Both cost an allocation and linear data movement per growth step, and neither produces a diagnostic. The reason the library will not simply move and roll back is that rollback is impossible — if the fourth element's move threw after three succeeded, the original range would already be partly moved from with no way to restore it.

writing.prompt: Write an `EventList` wrapping a `std::vector<std::string>` that documents a **stronger** postcondition than the library gives: after being moved from, an `EventList` is `empty()`, and callers may rely on it. Implement both move operations to deliver that guarantee, keep them `noexcept`, and explain in a comment why `= default` would not be enough. Separately, write a short function on a plain `std::string` annotating which operations on a moved-from object are allowed, which are allowed but unspecified, and which must not be relied on.
checklist: Both move operations are noexcept and explicitly clear() the source's vector after transferring from it
A comment states that a defaulted move would leave the member valid but unspecified, so the postcondition would not be guaranteed
The plain-string function marks assigning a fresh value and calling a precondition-free operation such as clear() as allowed
It marks relying on empty() after the move as not to be relied on, noting that implementations commonly do empty it
It shows the moved-from string being given a fresh value before any further use
writing.notes: The interesting part is that the `clear()` is almost always redundant — nearly every implementation already empties a moved-from vector — and that is exactly why you cannot skip it. The observation is real and unportable at the same time, so the only way to turn it into something callers may depend on is to write it down and enforce it. Note the direction of the promise: strengthening is allowed, and the standard's baseline of destructible-and-assignable is a floor, not a ceiling. Clang-Tidy's `bugprone-use-after-move` catches the common accidental read; it is conservative static analysis rather than a language rule.

writing.prompt: This `Playlist::add` was written with `std::move` specifically to avoid a copy, and it copies on every call. Explain in a comment exactly which overload runs and why, then fix the signature. Add a second method that only reads its argument, and a usage function showing what a prvalue, a named lvalue, an xvalue, and a `const` object each cost at the call site.
checklist: A comment states that std::move on a const std::string& yields const std::string&&, which cannot bind to std::string's move constructor, so the copy constructor is selected
A comment notes that std::move did produce an xvalue — the request was made and refused, not ignored
The fixed sink method takes std::string by value and moves it into storage
The read-only method takes const std::string& and performs no move
The usage function annotates the prvalue, lvalue, and xvalue call sites with their copy and move counts
The usage function shows std::move on a const object silently copying
writing.notes: The `const&` parameter plus `std::move` is a common review miss precisely because the `std::move` looks like the fix. It is worth being able to state the trade the by-value sink makes: it is strictly better for prvalue and xvalue callers, and one cheap move worse for a caller passing a named lvalue it intends to keep. Choose it when callers commonly hand over values they are finished with, and keep `const&` where the function only reads. The same reasoning explains the last line: do not add `const` to an object that must transfer ownership, because `std::move` preserves it.
